Neonates of the Peppered maskray enter the world at a disc width of 10 cm [Lb = 10 cm], a size that reflects the energetic constraints of gestation in this small dasyatid. Following a gestation period of approximately 305 days [ab = approximately 305 days] at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the free-swimming pups are immediately capable of benthic foraging. This protracted developmental interval is typical of elasmobranchs, where yolk-dependent embryogenesis proceeds slowly even at relatively warm temperatures. The comparatively large birth size relative to the adult female suggests a reproductive strategy centered on producing well-developed offspring rather than numerous small young, a pattern observed in several other Neotrygon species. Field surveys indicate that neonatal mortality is highest during the first few weeks post-parturition, when inexperienced pups must learn to locate buried invertebrate prey in the dynamic intertidal and shallow subtidal zones they inhabit along the northeastern Australian coastline.

A suite of life-history milestones has been documented for Peppered maskray populations under typical thermal conditions. Females attain sexual maturity at a disc width of approximately 18 cm [Lp = approximately 18 cm], whereas males achieve puberty at a slightly smaller size of about 17 cm [Lp = about 17 cm]. This subtle sexual dimorphism in maturation size is common among dasyatids and likely reflects differential selective pressures on body size relative to reproductive output. The ultimate disc width for the species reaches 27.5 cm [Li = 27.5 cm] in females, while males, being the smaller sex, attain a maximum disc width of 24 cm [Li = 24 cm]. These asymptotic sizes represent the point at which somatic growth effectively ceases, with further energy being directed toward reproduction and maintenance. The growth trajectory from a 10 cm neonate to these terminal dimensions is relatively rapid, allowing individuals to pass through the vulnerable juvenile stage quickly.

At a water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the Peppered maskray's reproductive output is realized through an annual cycle of a single litter, with each litter containing one to five pups [N_R_i = each litter containing one to five pups], and a frequency of one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. This results in a maximum annual reproductive output of one to five pups per year [Ri = one to five pups per year]. This comparatively low fecundity places the species firmly within the K-selected reproductive spectrum characteristic of elasmobranchs, where iteroparity and the production of a few, well-provisioned offspring are the norm. The capacity to store sperm from a single copulation allows females to fertilize successive litters without repeated mating, an adaptation that buffers against low encounter rates with males in the patchy coastal environments they occupy. Longitudinal studies in Moreton Bay have confirmed that not every mature female breeds annually, suggesting that reproductive output is modulated by local prey availability and female body condition.

The ultimate wet weight recorded for adult females of this species reaches 668 grams [Wwi = 668 grams], an allometrically consistent value given their 27.5 cm disc width and the robust body form typical of benthic stingrays. Males, which have a smaller ultimate disc width of 24 cm [Li = 24 cm], correspondingly attain a lower asymptotic body mass of 415 grams [Wwi = 415 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is reflected not only in disc dimensions but also in the thickness of the pectoral disc and the relative size of the tail, with females investing more heavily in body volume to accommodate ovarian development and gestation. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Neotrygon kuhlii reveal that the Peppered maskray achieves a more modest maximum mass, a difference that may be linked to its occupation of shallower, more energetically variable habitats. These mass estimates are derived from robust length-weight relationships validated across several independent field seasons.

The maximum lifespan of the Peppered maskray has been estimated at approximately 18 years [am = approximately 18 years] under the prevailing thermal regime of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], a longevity that is consistent with the species' slow pace of life and with other dasyatids of similar body size. This extended lifespan, coupled with late sexual maturation and low annual fecundity, renders the population particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as the removal of reproductively active adults cannot be quickly compensated by recruitment. Age determination using vertebral banding patterns has confirmed incremental growth throughout life, with the oldest individual recorded in a wild sample being a 17-year-old female. The species' benthic, site-attached lifestyle may reduce predation risk for adults, contributing to this elevated survivorship. In contrast, juvenile mortality is high, a demographic bottleneck that likely regulates population size in undisturbed habitats.
